textbookText: Oviducal funnel are large, saucer shaped structures with much folded and ciliated margin. They lie below each ovary in 13th segment. 3. Oviducts Each oviducal funnel posteriorly continues into a short conical and internally ciliated tube called oviduct. Two oviducts run posteriorly by penetrating the septum between 13th and 14th segment and finally unite to form a common oviduct. Now, common oviduct opens mid-ventrally to the exterior by a single opening in 14th segment which is called female genital opening. 4. Spermathecae There are altogether four pairs of small flask shaped structures called spermathecae in the segments 6th, 7th, 8th and 9th in ventro lateral position. Each spermatheca has a broad pear shaped part called ampulla and a short narrow neck with a blind caecum or diverticulum on its side. After copulation, the sperms are received and stored in the diverticulum. Ampulla provides nourishment to maintain live condition of sperms until the ovaries mature. Each pairs of spermathecae opens outside through spermathecal pores situated ventrolaterlly in the groove between segment 5/6, 6/7, 7/8 and 8/9.

8.3.8 COPULATION AND COCOON FORMATION Copulation: In earthworms, copulation generally takes place during rainy season in the month from July to October at night time which lasts for about an hour. At this time, two sexually mature earthworms attach themselves by their ventral surfaces with their anterior end facing opposite

Figure 8.3.22 coplaton in earthworm direction. In this condition, Male genital opening of one worm lies opposite to spermathecal pore of another worm. The area of male genital opening of each worm is raised into an elevated structure called the papilla which act as the copulatory organ and is inserted through spermathecal pore of another worm for the transfer of sperm. In this way, mutual transfer of sperms and prostatic fluid between copulating worms takes place and they become separate. Sperms are received and collected in spermathecae and maintained live until female reproductive organ matures. Cocoon formation: Cocoon formation takes place after the process of copulation, when ovaries become mature. The clitellar gland consists of mucous secreting gland, cocoon forming gland and albumen secreting gland. After the ovaries become mature, clitellum secrete a gluey or sticky substance which gets hardened on exposure of air to form a circular band or girdle around it. When the membranous girdle is formed, earthworm withdraws itself backwards from the girdle and several unfertilized ova are laid into the girdle through the female genital opening. As the girdle passes over the spermathecal pores, sperms from spermathecae are also shed off into the girdle. The girdle is finally thrown off from the anterior end and both ends of girdle or cocoon are closed due to its elastic wall. In this way, a light-yellow coloured, oval or rounded cocoon is formed which contains fertilized eggs along with nutritive albuminous substance secreted by albuminous gland. Many cocoons are formed in succession after each mating.

Figure 8.3.23 Cocoon formation in earthworm Fertilization is external and takes place in cocoon when it is deposited on land. Among many fertilized eggs in a cocoon, only one fertilized egg develops into new youngone. Cleavage of zygote is holoblastic, unequal and development is direct. A young earthworm thus formed escapes from cocoon in about 15-20 days. 8.3.9 ECONOMIC IMPORTANCE OF EARTHWORM Biology, Grade 11 | 377
